results.note: Numbers match. Denominators now named: 25.7% is of the 9,973 coded visits; 9.3% is of all 2,567 (9.8% of the 2,432 with a route). Source says cannabis use, not route, is assessed in nursing form and notes; adults added.
results.corrected_extracted: Chart review of all emergency visits to one Colorado university hospital, 1 January 2012 to 31 December 2016: 449,031 eligible visits, 9,973 with a cannabis-related diagnosis code (the participants were adults with such a code), 2,567 (25.7% of the 9,973) judged at least partly attributable to cannabis. Route was recorded in 2,432 of the 2,567 (94.7%): 238 edible (9.3% of the 2,567; 9.8% of the 2,432) and 2,194 inhaled; the 135 visits with insufficient documentation were counted as inhaled, giving 2,329. A dose was recorded in 130 (5.1%). Cannabis use is assessed in the nursing assessment questionnaire and the providers' notes; the route was captured from the medical record, and inhalation was presumed when it was not documented. Visits attributable to inhaled and to edible cannabis both rose each year (Figure 2, an image, not read).

results.note: All six rows match Table 2 (negative CIs reordered low to high). Recomputed shares agree; 43/238 is 18.07, printed 18.0. Row is 'Psychiatric symptoms' (overall). Inhaled group includes 135 presumed-inhaled visits. Tobacco: source silent.

Counts and shares match Table 2; 15.1, 14.5 and 20.7% recomputed. Fixed one attachment: 301 people and 440 visits are for cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome (17.1%), not all 788 gastrointestinal visits.
results.corrected_extracted: Table 2 counts, edible and inhaled: intoxication 115 and 647 (762 in all); acute psychiatric symptoms 43 and 254 (297); cardiovascular symptoms 19 and 73 (92); gastrointestinal symptoms 36 and 752; cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome 20 and 420. Editors' arithmetic: edible-attributed visits were 15.1%, 14.5% and 20.7% of the intoxication, acute psychiatric and cardiovascular visits, so most visits for those reasons were inhaled-attributed. Across the 2,567 visits (reasons not mutually exclusive): gastrointestinal symptoms including cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome 788 (30.7%), of which cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome 440 visits (17.1%) by 301 people; intoxication 762 (29.7%), psychiatric symptoms 633 (24.7%), cardiovascular symptoms 92 (3.6%).

results.note: All figures match the Results text and Table 1 (810/2,567 = 31.6% etc. recomputed). Percentages are of visits, not people. The hyperemesis explanation for admissions is the authors' impression, untested, as the anchor says.

Matches Discussion paragraph 1 closely. 'Lead to' is the authors' causal wording from a chart review; attribution is correct. The education statement is public-health advice, not advice on using a product.

Matches; recomputed 219/2,038 = 10.7%, 212/65,810 = 0.32%, ratio about 33. Sales side is flower plus edibles only (Table 3): concentrates absent, though inhaled visits cover every inhaled route. Authors judge home-grown and black-market supply minor.
Matches Discussion paragraph 5 and the Abstract limitation. Dose counts are chart-recorded study data, not advice. Presumed-inhalation coding bias is reported as the authors report it.

Corrected one label: the page names reference 8 only by title (Giombi 2018, consumers' perceptions), not as a survey. Timing figures match. Barrus puts inhaled peak effect at 20 to 30 minutes; Monte, peak blood level at 30 to 90.
results.corrected_extracted: Timing as described by the authors, citing a pharmacology review (Grotenhermen 2003, not read): inhaled cannabis gives clinical effects within 10 minutes, a peak blood concentration within 30 to 90 minutes and complete clearance within 4 hours; oral THC does not reach a significant blood concentration until at least 30 minutes, peaks at about 3 hours and clears about 12 hours after ingestion. People report longer-lasting effects with edibles than with smoking or vaping (reference 8, Giombi 2018, on consumers' perceptions of edibles; its design is not stated on the page) and more intense effects and unpleasant psychiatric symptoms (reference 9, an analysis of Twitter posts); neither was read. Death has been associated with edible products in three cases taken from news reports (references 10 to 12). No timing was measured in this study's patients.

results.note: Funder, grant numbers, both disclosures and the committee seat match; no industry or advocacy funding is printed. First author is Monte. The page's publisher disclaimer (views are the authors' own) is not in the anchor.

Corrected: Abstract compares ingestion with inhalation of cannabis extracts; anchor said only 'other methods'. 'Occasional paper' is not printed on the page (PMC lists Methods Rep RTI Press), so it is dropped. No methods section exists.
results.corrected_extracted: A narrative overview published by RTI Press (PMC lists it as Methods Rep RTI Press), written for the educated layperson and policy makers. The Abstract says little research has evaluated how ingestion differs from other methods of cannabis use in therapeutic efficacy, subjective effects and safety; that the most prominent difference between ingestion and inhalation of cannabis extracts is the delayed onset of drug effect with ingestion; and that consumers who do not understand this may consume more than intended before the effect starts, often resulting in profoundly adverse effects (no count is given). The Introduction says the authors describe promises and challenges and critically examine extant research; no search method, selection criteria or appraisal of studies is described.

results.note: Numbers match; source is the Colorado Department of Revenue annual update. The 45% is of 'total cannabis sales', measure not stated, so it is not comparable with Monte 2019's 0.32% by THC weight (Monte's 4.8 million 2014 edible units agree).

Corrected: the source says peak effect (not peak level) at 20 to 30 minutes and psychoactive effects tapering; 'sex' is 'gender' in the source. Not to be set against Monte's peak blood concentrations (30 to 90 minutes). All else matches.
results.corrected_extracted: After eating, liver first-pass metabolism forms 11-OH-THC, a potent psychoactive metabolite that appears in blood in higher quantities after ingestion than after inhalation (as cited); the authors write that it may be responsible for the stronger and longer-lasting effect of edibles compared with comparable doses of smoked cannabis. Inhaled THC takes initial effect within minutes and shows peak effect in about 20 to 30 minutes, with psychoactive effects tapering off within 2 to 3 hours; the initial psychoactive effect of edibles takes 30 to 90 minutes to be felt and the high is longer-lasting, with a peak 2 to 4 hours after ingestion (Grotenhermen 2003 and others, as cited, not read). Weight, metabolism, gender and eating habits are said to affect how soon and how long.

results.note: Quote exact. Corrected: source says 'likely due to'; the anchor dropped the hedge. 'Viewpoint' is on neither page. The statement gives no place, period or count; Monte 2019 Table 2 has edibles in 115 of 762 intoxication visits (15.1%).
results.corrected_extracted: After oral doses, plasma THC is lower than after smoking or infusion, and its correlation with degree of intoxication varies considerably across individuals (Hollister 1981, as cited); oral bioavailability is 6 to 10 percent of the amount in the product (Schwilke 2009, as cited). The authors say the lack of consistency and the delayed intoxication may lead both new and experienced people to take more than intended, and write that edible products are responsible for the majority of health care visits due to cannabis intoxication, which they say is likely due to users' failure to appreciate the delayed effects (a 2015 JAMA article by Monte, Zane and Heard, as cited, not read).

results.note: Corrected one label: Monte 2019's reference list marks Hudak 2015 as a letter; neither page calls it a case report, and the text says 'patients'. Rest matches. Describes patients' behaviour; not advice.
results.corrected_extracted: Dosage estimation for retail products may be inexact (Vandrey 2015, as cited). Anecdotal reports from medicinal cannabis patients are said to confirm that even people who take cannabis daily may consume more than expected (Hudak 2015, a letter in the American Journal of Psychiatry, as cited): having eaten the suggested serving first, patients ate the entire product after not feeling any effects, and found it practical to eat the entire product in one sitting.

results.note: Matches paragraph 14 (age, month, balcony, 60 minutes, 2 hours, autopsy wording). Reference is an MMWR Notes from the Field report. Anchor leaves out serving size and dose, which suits section 7; no advice wording.

Corrected scope: Colorado's mid-2014 labelling rule was for recreational edibles; it was not originally applied to medicinal cannabis. Vandrey figures match as printed; 'these products' leaves the base of 'more than half' unclear.
results.corrected_extracted: A 2014 newspaper investigation found the actual THC content of retail edibles often differed significantly from labels; from mid-2014 Colorado required THC in recreational edibles to be tested and labelled but tested only against a threshold, which does not check label accuracy. One study of medicinal edibles sold in California and Washington is reported to have found that the total THC content of 83 percent of edibles tested differed from the labelled amounts by over 10 percent, with more than half containing significantly less than claimed and nearly a quarter significantly more (Vandrey 2015, as cited; not read).

results.note: Corrected three wordings: the poison-centre figures concern unintentional exposures in children up to 9 years; the third group is 'nonlegal states'; the 2005 to 2009 hospital figure is accidental ingestion, not edible. All numbers match.
results.corrected_extracted: Children: in a review of US poison-centre data on unintentional exposures in young children (up to 9 years of age), cannabis-related calls rose 30.3 percent a year in decriminalized states, 11.5 percent in states undergoing transition to decriminalization and 1.5 percent in nonlegal states, 2005 to 2011 (Wang 2014, as cited), with similar increases in edible-related calls in 2013 to 2015 (Cao 2016, as cited). The authors write that emergency visits for child exposure remain relatively low: a Colorado children's hospital saw no cases of accidental ingestion in 2005 to 2009, eight children who ingested edible cannabis in 2013 and 14 in 2014 (a hospital-association web item, as cited). Visitors: out-of-town patient visits to an Aurora, Colorado hospital for problems after edibles almost doubled from 85 to 168 per 10,000 visits between 2013 and 2014, with no significant difference for Colorado residents (Kim 2016, as cited; not read); that study's authors attributed the rise to higher potency and visitors' unfamiliarity with edibles. The reference list gives the letter's authors as Kim, Hall, Genco, Van Dyke, Barker and Monte (the first author of Monte 2019 is Monte).

results.note: Corrected: 'habitual cannabis smoking'; added the source's comparison (edibles as opposed to smoking cannabis, particularly for conditions such as cancer). That uncited sentence reads as route-choice advice: the authors' wording; flag for the senior author.
results.corrected_extracted: On smoke: cannabis and tobacco smoke are said to be similar in kind in toxicity; cannabis smoke is linked to lung inflammation and bronchitis; the link to chronic lung disease is unclear; epidemiological research links habitual cannabis smoking to several cancers but is complicated by small samples and co-occurring tobacco smoking. The authors then write that eating edibles does not seem to affect lung function or raise cancer risk, calling this a solid rationale for choosing this route as opposed to smoking cannabis, particularly for medical conditions such as cancer. No study of people who eat cannabis is cited for the last point.

results.note: Acknowledgments text matches (RTI internal funds, NIDA grant DA-03672). Page metadata and biographies place all eight authors at RTI International. No conflict-of-interest, funder-role or disclosure statement appears on the page.
